(1) Bruhn 2006 is a TU Darmstadt preprint, and we do criticize Meyl for non-peer-reviewed venues elsewhere in the same paragraph — the surface parallel is real. (2) Q-factor resonant enhancement in bifilar coils is real physics: Tesla-style resonant coils can reach Q ~ 100+, and the 350 mV upper bound of the static-mutual-inductance calc can indeed scale to volts under resonance. Both angles need direct neutralization, not just implicit dismissal.

Even at that magnitude the signal remains within Maxwellian near-field bounds: resonant inductive coupling in the tens of volts is precisely what commercial Qi wireless-charging pads and NFC readers deliver at similar frequencies and short-range separations (WPC Qi specification v1.3.1; Weinstein & Lafontaine, IEEE Trans. Ind. Electron. 56(7), 2009). High-Q enhancement changes the amplitude, not the physics — it does not carry the observation out of the reactive near-field regime into a domain where scalar waves would be required.

anticipated_objections.objection: The Bruhn double-standard preempt still uses a preprint (Bruhn 2006) to refute Meyl. Isn't that circular?
anticipated_objections.response: The distinction is between what kind of claim requires what kind of evidence. Internal-consistency proofs are inspectable — a reader with the equations in hand can verify Bruhn's point about the E(r(t)) vs E(r,t) functional form themselves. Positive empirical claims (energy detected on the shielded side) require someone else's independent apparatus and measurement chain, which is what peer review gates. Same evidentiary standard applied to both means: internal-consistency proofs pass the inspection test on their own; positive empirical claims must clear replication. Bruhn passes his test; Meyl does not pass his.

anticipated_objections.objection: Q ~ 100 might be conservative — bifilar Tesla coils can reach Q ~ 300+ in some published designs, giving ~100 V.
anticipated_objections.response: Same argument scales: 100 V is still within Maxwellian near-field bounds. Qi wireless charging delivers up to 15 W at ~5–20 V rms into 50 Ω loads (roughly 100–400 mA); the underlying near-field mechanism is identical. High Q raises the amplitude but does not change the physical regime — the coil separation, wavelength, and distance-to-source ratio remain in the reactive-zone (d < λ/2π) regardless of how much energy the resonator stores per cycle. What would carry the observation out of Maxwellian near-field into scalar-wave territory is not a higher amplitude, but coupling at d >> λ/2π (true far field) or violation of the 1/r^3 reactive-zone falloff. Neither has been demonstrated.
